title: Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO offered 3 clues about where the AI trade goes next
excerpt: Anthropic's record debut showed strong investor appetite, but also underscored major concerns surrounding the AI trade.

Wall Street's blockbuster IPO trilogy is now two-thirds complete.

SpaceX set the stage this summer, Anthropic delivered the second installment on Thursday, and OpenAI is the much-anticipated finale waiting in the wings.

Anthropic's public-market debut was certainly a hit: It priced above range, opened 34% above its IPO price, and sealed a record $107 billion deal, including a separate private placement. Shares ended the day 17% higher.

But Wall Street gave the broader AI trade much harsher reviews. After a strong open on the heels of Anthropic's pricing the prior evening, investors sold the news.

It was ultimately a good day for Anthropic and a bad one for pretty much everyone else. Here are three takeaways from the AI titan's first day of trading:

1. The AI relief rally had no legs

AI stocks surged out of the gate on Thursday, with chipmakers, neoclouds, and the broader Nasdaq 100 posting meaningful early gains. But the rally disintegrated as the session wore on.

Notable movers included neocloud bellwether CoreWeave swinging from a double-digit gain into the red, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index sharply reversed after rising 5% in the first hour of trading.

Anthropic itself — similar to SpaceX in June — faded significantly from its $111.50 opening trade, even if it remained above the IPO price.

The trading session showed that the market still has even bigger concerns than the biggest IPO in history. For investors…

2. … The AI trade's biggest bills are still coming due

Let's start with what Anthropic's offering did clarify: Initial demand and the bigger-than-anticipated deal size showed there is still an enormous investor appetite for a premier AI asset.

But that doesn't solve the existential problem of return on AI investment. Anthropic has committed to spend roughly $900 billion of compute and infrastructure over time — not far from the entire company's market value at IPO time. How will that jibe with credit-market pressure, geopolitical risks, and — most importantly — concerns that spending will always outrun profits?

Put differently, Anthropic's IPO showed that Wall Street is still willing to finance AI. But it didn't show how AI plans to eventually pay for itself.

3. Wall Street continues to get pickier

One investing trend that's come to define the AI trade — at least in recent weeks and months — is a flight to quality. During recent bouts of market turbulence, the diversified AI companies with strong balance sheets and war chests of cash stayed strongly afloat.

The market's response to Anthropic's debut is an extension of that. A record IPO used to be the kind of event that could lift an entire complex of stocks. Now, investors are demanding company-specific proof before piling in. The AI boom has reached a more mature phase.

With Anthropic now firmly in the market as a pure-play AI stock, attention will soon shift to OpenAI, the final chapter in Wall Street's blockbuster IPO trilogy. Can the Sam Altman-led juggernaut have better luck breathing life into the AI trade?
